         22   LLP (“BABC”) and Sam David Smith a.k.a. S. David Smith (“Smith”) (collectively, “Defendants”)

         23   (Plaintiffs and Defendants are collectively referred to as the “Parties”).

         24                                              JURISDICTION

         25          1.      This Court has jurisdiction to hear and determine the claims presented in this suit

         26   pursuant to 28 U.S.C. § 1332(a)(1). The Parties are “citizens of different states,” and the amount in

         27   controversy exceeds the sum of $75,000, exclusive of interest and costs.

         28   ///

                                             COMPLAINT; DEMAND FOR JURY TRIAL

          1                                       DIVISIONAL ASSIGNMENT

          2          2.      Venue is proper in this District pursuant to 28 U.S.C. § 1391(b)(2) because a substantial

          3   part of the events giving rise to Plaintiffs’ claims occurred within this District.

          4                                                   PARTIES

          5          3.      Redondo is a limited liability company organized under the laws of the state of

          6   Delaware, with its principal place of business in Overland Park, Johnson County, Kansas.

          7          4.      Koetting is an individual who resides in the county of Johnson, Kansas.

          8          5.      Plaintiffs are informed and believe, and thereon allege, that BABC is a limited liability

          9   partnership organized under the laws of the state of Alabama, with its principal place of business in

         10   Birmingham, Jefferson County, Alabama.

         11          6.      Plaintiffs are informed and believe, and thereon allege, that Smith is an individual who

         12   resides in Houston, Texas, is an attorney licensed to practice law in the state of Texas, and who at all

         13   times relevant, served as a partner of BABC.

         14          7.      Each defendant was the agent, alter-ego, employee, principal, partner, joint venturer,

         15   employer, or in some other capacity derivatively responsible for each of the acts of the other defendants.

         16                                         STATEMENT OF FACTS

         17   A.             Background Of The Tribal Lending Entity Agreement

         18          8.      In August of 2013, Redondo entered into a Consultant and Independent Contractor

         19   Agreement (the “Tribe Agreement”) with Clear Loan Solutions (“CLS”), a tribal lending entity

         20   (“TLE”) organized under the laws of the federally-recognized Native American tribe called Big Lagoon

         21   Rancheria (“Big Lagoon”).

         22          9.      Koetting previously operated consumer lending platforms and brought over a decade of

         23   experience, as well as consumer information and leads, which were then used to develop and expand

         24   the consumer lending business governed by the Tribe Agreement.

         25   ///

         26   ///

         27   ///

         28   ///

                                                                     2
976845
                                              COMPLAINT; DEMAND FOR JURY TRIAL
                    Case 1:24-cv-06104-RMI Document 1 Filed 08/28/24 Page 3 of 16




          1          10.     Under the Tribe Agreement, Redondo would serve as the executive director of CLS,

          2   managing the day-to-day operations of the consumer lending platform, including marketing, generating

          3   leads, underwriting, and loan servicing for and on behalf of CLS. Redondo arranged for the monies to

          4   fund the loan program through a related company and generated the leads and arranged for affiliates to

          5   put up the capital to finance loans made through the consumer lending platform.

          6          11.     Plaintiffs allege on information and belief, that one purpose of the Tribe Agreement was

          7   to allow consumer lending programs to be created that are qualified for sovereign immunity afforded

          8   to Big Lagoon. Native American tribes are allowed to do this via compliance with an “arm of the tribe”

          9   analysis which essentially requires the tribe to pass a tribal lending code, create a TLE wholly owned

         10   by the tribe, with the tribe exercising some control over the tribal entity and establishing a program to

         11   ensure compliance with the tribal lending code.

         12          12.     Under the Tribe Agreement, CLS and Big Lagoon were charged with complying with

         13   the arm of the tribe requirements.

         14          13.     Throughout the negotiation of the Tribe Agreement and after, Redondo received legal

         15   advice from Jennifer Galloway, a Florida attorney, who Plaintiffs allege on information and belief was

         16   then operating as a solo practitioner in the State of Florida through her professional association, Jennifer

         17   Galloway, P.A. (“Galloway”). Galloway negotiated and participated in drafting the Tribe Agreement

         18   for Redondo. Plaintiffs allege on information and belief that CLS was also represented by counsel in

         19   negotiating the Tribe Agreement.

         20          14.     In 2017, the relationship between CLS and Redondo became contentious and ultimately

         21   terminated on January 8, 2018 when CLS issued a termination letter.

         22          15.     CLS then took control of all bank accounts associated with and used to operate the loan

         23   program, even though they contained monies raised by and belonging to Redondo.

         24          16.     Similarly, Koetting’s brother, Daniel Koetting (“Dan”), operated a nearly identical

         25   relationship with a separate TLE, Green Gate Services, LLC (“Green Gate Services”) (also under Big

         26   Lagoon’s control), by and through an entity called Rockhill Consulting Group, LLC (“Rockhill”) (the

         27   Green Gate-Rockhill relationship referred herein as the “Rockhill Operation”). At all times, Koetting

         28   and Dan kept all operations separate and there was no overlap between Redondo and Rockhill.

                                                                     3
976845
                                              COMPLAINT; DEMAND FOR JURY TRIAL
                     Case 1:24-cv-06104-RMI Document 1 Filed 08/28/24 Page 4 of 16




          1   Plaintiffs allege on information and belief that the Rockhill Operation was significantly larger than

          2   Redondo. Plaintiffs estimate that Redondo and CLS’s loan program was approximately 30% the size

          3   of the Rockhill Operation.

          4   B.             Retention Of BABC

          5           17.    Upon the termination of the Tribe Agreement, Galloway advised Plaintiffs to retain

          6   counsel. Galloway provided only one recommendation and insisted Plaintiffs retain BABC, and Smith

          7   specifically. On January 10, 2018, Plaintiffs and BABC entered into an Attorney Client Engagement

          8   Agreement, a copy of which is attached hereto as Exhibit 1 and is incorporated herein by reference.

          9   The Attorney Client Engagement Agreement includes an implied term that BABC would meet the

         10   standard of care. Galloway served as Plaintiffs’ co-counsel for Plaintiffs, until the representation was

         11   consolidated when Galloway joined BABC as a partner in or about April or May 2018.

         12           18.    There is no written engagement agreement between Koetting and Defendants.

         13   Nevertheless, Defendants served as Koetting’s attorney in the dispute with CLS. Accordingly, on

         14   information and belief, Plaintiffs allege that Koetting and Defendants entered into an implied-in-fact

         15   contract for Defendants to represent Koetting. That implied-in-fact contract included the following

         16   terms: (a) Defendants would represent Koetting in the dispute with CLS; (b) Defendants would meet

         17   the standard of care; (c) Defendants would bill reasonable Koetting on an hourly basis at reasonable

         18   rates; and (d) Koetting would pay for Defendants’ services, so long as they met the terms of the

         19   implied-in-fact contract.

         20           19.    At the same time Defendants represented Plaintiffs in the dispute with CLS, Defendants

         21   also represented Dan and Rockhill in the dispute with Green Gate Services. At no time did Defendants

         22   advise Plaintiffs of any actual or potential conflict of interest that could arise out of the representation

         23   of Koetting, Redondo, Dan, and/or Rockhill, and Defendants did not get Plaintiffs’ informed written

         24   consent to represent all those parties, even though there were potential and possibly actual conflicts

         25   of interest.

         26   C.             Underlying Arbitration

         27           20.    On or about January 8, 2018, CLS filed a demand for arbitration with the American

         28   Arbitration Association (“AAA”) against Redondo and Koetting personally, including claims for

                                                                     4
976845
                                              COMPLAINT; DEMAND FOR JURY TRIAL
                     Case 1:24-cv-06104-RMI Document 1 Filed 08/28/24 Page 5 of 16




          1   breach of fiduciary duty, fraud, conversion/theft, misuse of consumer data (Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act),

          2   breach of contract, violation of the BLR Consumer Financial Services Regulatory Code, and alter ego

          3   asserting that Koetting and Redondo are one in the same. On or about February 14, 2018, Redondo

          4   filed a counter demand for arbitration against CLS for multiple breaches of the Tribe Agreement.

          5           21.      Even though the Tribe Agreement contains only a permissive arbitration clause under

          6   section 8(a)(ii), which provides that either party “may” refer disputes regarding their Tribe Agreement

          7   to arbitration under the rules of the American Arbitration Association, Defendants never advised

          8   Plaintiffs that conventional litigation was an option (and probably a much better option) and never

          9   explained the differences (procedurally or substantively) between arbitration and conventional

         10   litigation.

         11           22.      Plaintiffs are informed and believe that at no time did Defendants evaluate Plaintiffs’

         12   claims and/or defenses in the arbitration and did not advise Plaintiffs of the chances of success at

         13   arbitration. Plaintiffs are further informed and believe that at no time throughout the arbitration did

         14   Defendants update Plaintiffs as to the chances of success, nor did Defendants ever advise of alternative

         15   options or early resolution. Rather, Defendants always exuded positivity and all but guaranteed success,

         16   despite almost nothing but grim and disappointing results.

         17           23.      Pursuant to the Tribe Agreement, on or about March 22, 2018, CLS and Plaintiffs

         18   participated in a mediation. Plaintiffs are informed and believe that Defendants filed to ensure that

         19   representatives from Big Lagoon and/or CLS with settlement authority would be present at

         20   the mediation.

         21           24.      The mediation concluded without resolution.

         22           25.      After the failed mediation, Plaintiffs, Dan, Rockhill, and CLS and Green Gate Services

         23   began to select an arbitrator. CLS and Green Gate Services are collectively referred to as the “TLEs.”

         24   Plaintiffs, Dan, Rockhill, and the TLEs agreed to allow Gordon Netzorg (“Netzorg”) to act as the

         25   arbitrator based on the strong recommendation of Smith and Galloway.

         26   ///

         27   ///

         28   ///

                                                                    5
976845
                                              COMPLAINT; DEMAND FOR JURY TRIAL
                     Case 1:24-cv-06104-RMI Document 1 Filed 08/28/24 Page 6 of 16




          1          26.      Plaintiffs allege on information and believe that Netzorg previously worked for and/or

          2   with CLS’s counsel and had practiced in representing Native American tribes. Plaintiffs allege on

          3   information and believe that that Defendants failed to properly vet Netzorg’s background before

          4   recommending him as an arbitrator. Defendants did not ever advise Plaintiffs of these obvious conflicts.

          5          27.      On May 7, 2018, at a preliminary hearing, BABC agreed to an expedited scheduling

          6   order, setting the arbitration for September 10, 2018. Of note, BABC also agreed to consolidate claims

          7   between Plaintiffs and CLS to be heard with the claims between Green Gate Services and Dan

          8   and Rockhill.

          9          28.      On information and belief, Defendants did not advise Plaintiffs as to the benefits or

         10   pitfalls of consolidating these two cases, and Defendants did not seek permission from Plaintiffs to

         11   consolidate the matters. Plaintiffs allege on information and belief that Defendants unilaterally

         12   consolidated the arbitrations for their own convenience.

         13          29.      Plaintiffs allege on information and belief that consolidation was a poor strategic

         14   decision given that Redondo and Rockhill had no operating overlap, and Rockhill significantly

         15   overshadowed Redondo in terms of size of the loan operations. Plaintiffs allege on information and

         16   belief that Big Lagoon was more concerned with the alleged breaches in the Rockhill Operation.

         17          30.      On May 18, 2018, Defendants filed a Motion Relating to Joinder of Parties (“Joinder

         18   Motion”), seeking to dismiss Koetting and Dan from the arbitration on the ground that they were not

         19   parties to the respective contracts with the TLEs. Despite full access to documents and other supportive

         20   evidence, the Joinder Motion was woefully insufficient. In contrast, the TLEs’ opposition to the Joinder

         21   Motion was packed full of detailed alter ego allegations and documentary support as to Dan and

         22   Rockhill but lacked significant evidence regarding Koetting and Redondo. Plaintiffs allege on

         23   information and belief that despite this lack of evidence that Koetting and Redondo were alter egos,

         24   Defendants failed to effectively raise this weakness to combat the opposition, and the arbitrator denied

         25   the Joinder Motion. Ultimately, the arbitrator ruled that the claims against Koetting, personally,

         26   would proceed.

         27   ///

         28   ///

                                                                   6
976845
                                             COMPLAINT; DEMAND FOR JURY TRIAL
                     Case 1:24-cv-06104-RMI Document 1 Filed 08/28/24 Page 7 of 16




          1          31.     Plaintiffs allege on information and belief that Defendants failed to evaluate the alter

          2   ego allegations and did not take them seriously. Even after the ruling on the Joinder Motion, Plaintiffs

          3   allege on information and belief that Defendants ignored the gravity of the arbitrator’s ruling and

          4   assured Plaintiffs that everything would be put in the “proper context” at the arbitration.

          5          32.     Between the scheduling order and the arbitration hearing, Plaintiffs allege on

          6   information and belief that Defendants did little to prepare for arbitration. Plaintiffs allege on

          7   information and belief that Defendants waited until July 2018 to begin serving basic discovery on

          8   behalf of Plaintiffs and left no time for any follow up discovery. Plaintiffs allege on information and

          9   belief that Defendants did not take any depositions.

         10          33.     When it came to discovery issued to Plaintiffs, Plaintiffs allege on information and

         11   belief that Defendants waited until the last-minute to prepare responses and request necessary

         12   information, often causing Plaintiffs to work late nights and up to the deadlines to provide information

         13   and documents. Plaintiffs allege on information and belief that this last-minute work caused Defendants

         14   to produce documents and responses without review or concern for privacy or privilege protections.

         15          34.     Additionally, despite the clear indication that experts were necessary, Defendants failed

         16   to engage or hire any experts to present testimony at the arbitration.

         17          35.     In August 2018, Defendants first advised that they would “need some additional time to

         18   pull together information to be able to present our case. It is [Defendants] recommend [sic] that we ask

         19   the arbitrator to move the hearing to November.” On August 21, 2018, three weeks short of the

         20   arbitration, Defendants filed a request to continue the arbitration to November.

         21          36.     In the request, Defendants stated, “Based on the current state of discovery, it has become

         22   evident that this case is not ready for Arbitration in September. In addition to the above, neither party

         23   has taken depositions, designated experts, etc.” Defendants conceded: “At this point, it is just not

         24   possible to prepare this case for hearing in three weeks.”

         25          37.     On August 26, 2018, the arbitrator denied the request for continuance. In his ruling, the

         26   arbitrator found that there was no good cause for a continuance, stating:

         27   ///

         28   ///

                                                                     7
976845
                                             COMPLAINT; DEMAND FOR JURY TRIAL
                    Case 1:24-cv-06104-RMI Document 1 Filed 08/28/24 Page 8 of 16




          1                   [M]uch of the compression of the time available for discovery has
                              been caused by Claimants’ own substantial delay in making timely
          2                   disclosures. This is not a finding of wrongdoing, but it is a
                              determination that Claimants have caused much of the delay
          3
                              which they argue results in this case not being ready for
          4                   arbitration in September.

          5   (emphasis added)

          6           38.     Defendants caused the referenced delay.

          7           39.     On the same day arbitrator denied the request for a continuance, Galloway, then an

          8   attorney with BABC, conveyed a settlement proposal from both TLEs, settling all claims in the

          9   arbitration for $2.5 million. Plaintiffs allege on information and belief that BABC advised against

         10   accepting this offer or even making a counterproposal.

         11           40.     The denial of the continuance left Defendants with just two weeks to prepare for the

         12   hearing, without having taken a single deposition, in the absence of experts to present an accounting,

         13   damages or arm of the tribe analysis, and with no damage model.

         14           41.     Defendants did next to nothing to prepare Koetting to testify at the arbitration, on his

         15   personal behalf and on Redondo’s behalf, spending as little as one hour with Koetting. Neither Smith,

         16   nor Galloway, explained the process of presenting testimony, or presented Koetting with documents or

         17   notes, nor did they engage in any mock examinations. Late the night before the arbitration Smith tried

         18   to remedy this failure, but it was far too late to do so.

         19           42.     Plaintiffs allege on information and belief that Defendants focused their little

         20   preparation on Plaintiffs’ affirmative claims, and little to no time preparing to defend against the TLEs’

         21   claims, especially the alter ego allegations. Plaintiffs allege on information and belief that Defendants

         22   were more focused on their representation of Dan and Rockhill, not Plaintiffs.

         23           43.     Just before arbitration commenced, Defendants informed Plaintiffs that a key witness,

         24   Galloway, would not appear as a witness on Plaintiffs’ behalf, despite that she was to serve as

         25   co-counsel at the arbitration. This was surprising because Galloway was the attorney who negotiated

         26   the Tribe Agreement and advised Redondo throughout its relationship with CLS. Smith advised that

         27   Galloway was ill. Plaintiffs allege on information and belief that Galloway did not want to testify under

         28   oath due to an unrelated personal matter because testifying might expose her to liability. On information

                                                                      8
976845
                                              COMPLAINT; DEMAND FOR JURY TRIAL
                     Case 1:24-cv-06104-RMI Document 1 Filed 08/28/24 Page 9 of 16




          1   and belief, Plaintiffs allege that Defendants did not take any steps to secure Galloways’ testimony by

          2   videotape, deposition, or declaration.

          3          44.     Once Netzorg heard of Galloway’s unavailability, he offered a continuance. Over

          4   Plaintiffs’ objection, Smith declined the continuance.

          5          45.     BABC and Smith did not disclose anything to Plaintiffs regarding the conflict of interest

          6   that arose between their clients’ interests and Galloway’s interests in not testifying under oath.

          7          46.     The arbitration was an unmitigated disaster. Defendants’ lack of preparation was

          8   apparent from the outset. Plaintiffs allege on information and belief that Defendants failed to object to

          9   the TLEs’ “expert,” failed to object to the presentation of a speculative damage model, failed to present

         10   the evidence necessary to prove Plaintiffs’ defenses and failed to rebut the alter ego allegations.

         11          47.     Plaintiffs allege on information and belief that the TLEs’ expert relied almost

         12   exclusively on documents and information related to Rockhill and Dan and offered little evidence

         13   regarding Redondo and Koetting. Despite this failure, Plaintiffs allege on information and belief that

         14   Defendants did not discredit the evidence or object to it on Plaintiffs’ behalf.

         15          48.     Plaintiffs allege on information and belief that Defendants’ failure to properly prepare

         16   Koetting for examination lead to a devastating cross-examination.

         17          49.     The arbitration hearing concluded on September 12, 2018. The arbitrator permitted the

         18   parties to file closing briefs. Plaintiffs allege on information and belief that Defendants’ closing brief

         19   was woefully insufficient. Among other failures, Defendants did not adequately rebut the arguments

         20   and evidence the TLEs presented including the TLEs’ damages analysis and the differences between

         21   Plaintiffs and the Rockhill Operation.

         22          50.     Following an adverse interim award, Netzorg issued the final adverse ruling on

         23   December 26, 2018. The final ruling found wholly for the TLEs, denied all of Plaintiffs’ claims, and

         24   found Koetting as an alter ego of Redondo, and therefore personally liable. Netzorg awarded damages

         25   in favor of the TLEs and against Plaintiffs totaling $3,159,443, attorney fees in the amount of

         26   $193,822.50, and prejudgment interest on the combined amount of 7.25% per annum, from

         27   May 31, 2018 until paid.

         28   ///

                                                                    9
976845
                                             COMPLAINT; DEMAND FOR JURY TRIAL
                     Case 1:24-cv-06104-RMI Document 1 Filed 08/28/24 Page 10 of 16




          1           51.    After the final award, Defendants tried to address issues in the final award, via a Motion

          2   for Modification. In support, Defendants presented a report prepared by an expert that Plaintiffs insisted

          3   that Defendants retain. Plaintiffs allege on information and belief that the expert concluded that

          4   Plaintiffs’ liability was much less than the final award—approximately in the range of

          5   $100,000-$300,000.

          6           52.    Plaintiffs allege on information and belief that this belated expert-supported evidence

          7   should have been presented during the Arbitration.

          8           53.    Netzorg summarily denied the motion since it sought a redetermination of the merits,

          9   not correction of “clerical, typographical, or computational errors” allowed to be addressed by such

         10   motions under AAA Rules.

         11   D.             The Subsequent State Court Action And Appeals

         12           54.    The TLEs filed a Petition to Confirm the Arbitration Award in the Humboldt County

         13   Superior Court in a case entitled Green Gate Services, LLC et al., v. Dan Koetting, et al., Humboldt

         14   County Superior Court, Case No. CV190030 (the “State Court Action”). BABC’s attorneys appeared

         15   pro hac vice in the State Court Action for Plaintiffs, Dan, and Rockhill.

         16           55.    Defendants’ attempts in the State Court Action to get Koetting and Dan dismissed and

         17   avoid personal liability as alter egos were unsuccessful. On July 11, 2019, the Superior Court entered

         18   judgment against Plaintiffs, Dan, and Rockhill.

         19           56.    Plaintiffs, Dan, and Rockhill appealed the judgment.

         20           57.    Plaintiffs allege on information and belief that while the appeal was pending, the TLEs

         21   assigned their rights, title, and interest in the judgment to another tribal entity called

         22   JPV I, L.P. (“JPV”).

         23           58.    Plaintiffs allege on information and belief that confirmation of the judgment as to the

         24   individuals, including Koetting, has been marred with appeals (see e.g. JPV 1 L.P. v. Koetting,

         25   88 Cal. App. 5th 172 (2023)), and has yet to be confirmed. However, in April 2024, the case was

         26   remanded back to the Superior Court, and Plaintiffs anticipate that judgment will be entered against

         27   Plaintiffs soon.

         28   ///

                                                                   10
976845
                                             COMPLAINT; DEMAND FOR JURY TRIAL
                     Case 1:24-cv-06104-RMI Document 1 Filed 08/28/24 Page 11 of 16




          1   E.              Plaintiffs Would Have Received A Better Result At Arbitration

          2           59.     Plaintiffs would have obtained a better result if Defendants had acted as reasonably

          3   careful attorneys.

          4           60.     The same harm would not have occurred anyway without Defendants’ conduct.

          5           61.     Plaintiffs allege on information and belief that Defendants fell below the standard of

          6   care as alleged in this complaint. Among other mistakes, Defendants failed to: (a) competently evaluate

          7   the conflicts of interest triggered by Defendants’ representation of all Plaintiffs, Dan, and Rockhill and

          8   obtain Plaintiffs’ informed written consent to accept the representation; (b) competently evaluate the

          9   strengths of the claims raised against Plaintiffs and advise Plaintiffs what to do about those claims;

         10   (c) competently evaluate Plaintiffs’ risks of losing and competently advise Plaintiffs about settlement;

         11   (d) competently evaluate and present Plaintiffs’ claims; (e) competently prepare for arbitration and

         12   present Plaintiffs’ case; and (f) competently evaluate the alter ego allegations against Plaintiffs and

         13   advise Plaintiffs of same.

         14           62.     Alternatively, Plaintiffs allege on information and belief that had Defendants

         15   competently prepared for the arbitration (including conducting sufficient discovery, taking depositions,

         16   designating experts) and competently presented Plaintiffs’ case, then Plaintiffs would have prevailed

         17   at the arbitration.

         18           63.     Absent Defendants’ negligence the damages awarded against Plaintiffs would have

         19   been far less, and the arbitrator would not have imposed alter ego liability upon Koetting. Further,

         20   Plaintiffs allege on information and belief that Defendants’ negligence cost Plaintiffs substantial

         21   amounts to mitigate the damages, attorney’s fees and other costs in the State Court Action, the bond,

         22   and the appeals.

         23           64.     Plaintiffs allege on information and belief that as a proximate result of Defendants’

         24   wrongful conduct herein alleged, Plaintiffs have suffered damages of no less than $5 million.

         25           65.     Plaintiffs allege on information and belief that Defendants’ services in the arbitration

         26   were of little to no value, and Defendants should also disgorge the fees Plaintiffs paid them.
